Fifty Rupees, Two Seconds

How does UPI work?

WhatWhyWhenHowWhereWho

A drawing. Not a real code.

1OpeningEdition 3 · 10 October 2026

Rudyard Kipling once wrote about six honest serving men who taught him everything he knew. Their names were What and Why and When and How and Where and Who.

What really happens when a phone scans a QR code at a shop? Where does the money go? Why does it need something in the middle? When did India start paying like this, and how is it all over before you can count to three? And who makes all of it work?

Let's find out.

✦✦✦

The Speaker on the Counter

Picture a small Udupi restaurant in Bengaluru. It is half past eight on a Saturday morning. Upstairs is a hall with tables, where families come for a proper dinner. Down here there are no chairs. People stand at steel counters with plates of idli, and nobody stays longer than ten minutes.

At the front, a man sits behind a cash counter. A queue runs out of the door. Next to his elbow is a small speaker, about the size of a lunch box.

A woman holds her phone over the QR code stuck to the counter. She taps. She does not show him her screen. He does not ask.

One. Two.

The speaker talks. "Received fifty rupees."

He hands her a token. She is already walking to the counter. The next person steps up.

No note changed hands. No coin. Nobody counted anything. So what just happened?

2WhatPip · The Six

Nothing Moved

You have seen this a hundred times. At the vegetable cart. At the stationery shop. At the auto stand. A phone, a QR code, a beep.

It looks like the phone sent money to the shop. It did not.

Think about cash for a moment. A ₹50 note is a thing. You can fold it. You can lose it. When you hand it over, it leaves your hand and lands in another. You have it, or you do not.

Now think about the woman at the restaurant. Her money is not in her phone. It is not in her pocket either. It is in her bank account. And a bank account is not a locker with her notes inside. It is a balance. A number the bank keeps for her.

When she tapped, her balance went down by 50.

The restaurant has a bank account too, probably at a completely different bank. Its balance went up by 50.

That is all. Two balances changed at two banks. Nothing travelled down a road.

But here is the thing. Those two banks do not share a building. They may not share a city. Somebody had to tell both of them, at the same moment, and both had to agree.

And it is not happening once. In September 2026, India made 24.07 billion of these payments. That is more than 800 million a day. More than 9,000 every second, all day and all night.

Something to think about

If you never touch your money, is it still easy to know how much you have?

What is UPI?

UPI stands for Unified Payments Interface. Unified means joined together. It joins hundreds of banks so that any one of them can pay any other.

3Where / WhyPip · The Six

The Shortest Trip in India

So where did the ₹50 go?

If you tried to draw it on a map of India, you would have a problem. There is no road. There is no van. What travelled was a message. It made four stops.

  1. The phone. The app reads the QR code. Now it knows who is being paid.
  2. The switch. The message goes to one place that every bank in the system is connected to. It is run by the National Payments Corporation of India. Most people call it NPCI.
  3. Her bank. The switch asks one question. Does she have ₹50? Her bank checks her balance and takes 50 away.
  4. The restaurant's bank. The switch tells it to add 50. It does. A message goes back the other way. The speaker talks.

Four stops. And the woman has not put her phone away yet.

Why does it need the stop in the middle? Why can her bank not just talk to the restaurant's bank?

Try it with your class. Say there are 30 of you. Every one of you wants a private string telephone to every other person. How many strings is that? It is 435. The room would be a spider web.

Now do it another way. Everyone runs one string to the class monitor. The monitor passes messages on. That is 30 strings.

UPI has 703 banks. If every bank needed its own line to every other bank, that would be 246,753 lines. With one switch in the middle, it is 703.

That is the "where" of UPI. It is not a place on the map. It is the middle of the web.

But here is the strange part. When the speaker said "Received fifty rupees", the two banks had not actually paid each other. Not yet. That comes later, and Page 5 is where you will see it.

Something to think about

UPI works because every bank trusts one middle point. What else in your life works only because everyone trusts the same middle point?

Try it: strings in the classroom

703 banks. 246,753 lines, or 703.

Meanwhile, outside India

India is not the only country that pays like this. Brazil has a system called Pix. It started in 2020 and is run by Brazil's central bank.

And UPI itself has left home. By 30 June 2026 you could scan and pay with UPI at shops in ten countries: the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, France, Mauritius, Nepal, Bhutan, Qatar, Sri Lanka, Cambodia and Greece.

4When / HowPip · The Six

How India Got Here

Here is something most grown-ups get wrong. They think UPI was the first way to send money instantly in India. It was not.

Start in 2010.

22 November 2010 · Instant, but fiddly

A service called IMPS begins. For the first time, money can go from one bank to another at any hour, even on a Sunday. But you need the other person's account number and an 11-character bank code called an IFSC. Now picture reading that out across a noisy counter with a queue behind you. Nobody is paying for idli that way.

11 April 2016 · The test run

UPI is switched on, but only as a trial. The Governor of the Reserve Bank of India announces it in Mumbai. There are 21 banks, and the people testing it are mostly the banks' own staff. The big idea is simple. No account number. No bank code. Just a short address, a bit like an email address for money.

25 August 2016 · The doors open

Now ordinary customers can use it. But not every bank gets in. A bank first had to prove itself in the trial: 1,000 test customers, 5,000 payments, and about 8 out of 10 of them going through properly. These are two separate dates. April was the test. August was the start.

8 November 2016 · Cash runs short

The old ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes stop being valid. For some weeks, cash is hard to get. Many people try paying by phone for the first time. You can see it in the numbers. In August 2016, its first month with customers, UPI carried about 93,000 payments. In December 2016 it carried about 2 million. In January 2017, more than 4 million.

30 December 2016 · One app for everyone

The Prime Minister launches an app called BHIM, built on UPI. Now hold on to that December 2016 number. About 2 million payments in a month.

Because in September 2026 it was 24.07 billion. Roughly twelve thousand times more.

So who was paying for all this?

Until December 2019 · Shops paid a little

When a customer paid by UPI, the shop's bank could keep a small slice. Up to 30 paise on every ₹100. That slice has a name: the merchant discount rate, or MDR.

1 January 2020 · The slice goes to zero

The government says no MDR on UPI. Shops now receive every rupee. But running the switch, the apps and the banks' computers still costs money. From 2021 the government starts paying banks a small amount for handling small UPI payments.

Then the numbers kept growing. And the question came back.

Three dates in 2026 · Do not mix them up

On 4 August 2026, Parliament changed the law that had kept the slice at zero. On 15 September 2026, NPCI published the details. And NPCI set 15 October 2026 as the date for the new slice to begin: 40 paise on every ₹100, only on payments above ₹2,000, and only at bigger shops. Then traders and payment companies asked for more time. On 9 October 2026, NPCI was weighing whether to wait until 1 January 2027.

The ₹50 plate of idli? Nothing changes. Not for her, and not for the restaurant.

The family dinner upstairs is another story. That is on Page 6.

  • 22 Nov 2010IMPS begins
  • 11 Apr 2016UPI trial, 21 banks
  • 25 Aug 2016Open to customers
  • 8 Nov 2016Old ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes withdrawn
  • 30 Dec 2016BHIM app
  • Dec 2019Last month of the old MDR
  • 1 Jan 2020Zero MDR
  • 4 Aug 2026Law changed
  • 15 Sep 2026NPCI publishes details
  • 15 Oct 2026New MDR due, or wait until 1 Jan 2027?
What is a slice of 40 paise?

On a ₹3,000 bill it is ₹12. On a ₹50 bill it would be 20 paise, but small bills are not charged at all.

5HowPip · The Six

Six Steps in Two Seconds

Count to two. All of this has already happened.

STEP 1

The Scan

The phone reads the QR code. The code holds the restaurant's UPI address. It does not hold its account number.

STEP 2

The PIN

She types her secret number. It is scrambled before it leaves the phone, so nobody along the way can read it.

STEP 3

The Question

The request reaches the NPCI switch. The switch works out which bank is hers and passes the question on.

STEP 4 · THE TURNING POINT

The Check

Her bank checks two things. Is the PIN right? Is there ₹50 in the account? If yes, it takes the ₹50. If no, everything stops here.

STEP 5

The Credit

The switch tells the restaurant's bank. That bank adds ₹50 to the restaurant's account.

STEP 6

The Ping

The answer runs back the way it came. Her phone shows a tick. The speaker on the counter talks.

A bank is allowed up to 15 seconds to answer. That has been the rule since 16 June 2025. Most of the time it feels like two.

Later that day

The Settling Up

Here is the part nobody sees. When the speaker talked, her bank had not yet paid the restaurant's bank. All day, payments fly in both directions between hundreds of banks. So ten times a day, NPCI adds everything up. Each bank then pays, or receives, only the difference. One big sum instead of millions of tiny ones.

Something to think about

The speaker says the money came. Why does the man at the counter believe it?

6WhoPip · The Six

Who Makes It Work?

Count the players. There are more than two.

You The person paying. You pay ₹0 for using UPI. That stays true after the new slice begins.

The two banks Hers and the restaurant's. They are two of 703. Each one runs computers that must answer in seconds, at any hour, on any day.

The apps The app on her phone is not her bank. It is a front door to it. There are many such apps. A few carry a very large share of the payments. Many carry only a little.

NPCI The switch in the middle. It was set up in December 2008 by the Reserve Bank of India and the Indian Banks' Association. It is owned by banks, and it is not run to make a profit.

The shop And this is where the story gets interesting.

✦✦✦

Go back to the restaurant. Before the speaker arrived, UPI was slower than cash at the counter. A customer paid and held up a phone. "See, it went through." Was it today's payment? Was it even real? Some people used apps to make fake payment screens, and shopkeepers got cheated. So the man at the counter checked his own phone for a message from his bank, while the queue grew.

The first soundbox appeared in 2019. It speaks only when the restaurant's own payment company tells it the money has arrived. So the speaker is not a gadget. It is the answer to a question: how do I know?

✦✦✦

Now walk upstairs. It is Saturday night in the dining hall. A family of eight has finished dinner. The bill is ₹3,200. Someone scans the QR code. The speaker talks.

Under the old rule, the restaurant receives ₹3,200. Once the new slice begins, it receives ₹3,187.20. The missing ₹12.80 is the MDR, the slice from Page 4. There is a little tax on top of that slice too.

The family pays ₹3,200 either way. The rule says a shop cannot add the slice to the customer's bill.

Now look at how narrow this rule is.

  • Send money to a friend or a cousin. No slice.
  • Pay a small shop that takes in up to ₹1 lakh a month by UPI. No slice, even on a big bill. That covers the vegetable cart and the tea stall.

NPCI says about 96 out of every 100 payments to shops will see no change at all.

So why have the slice? NPCI says the money will go into keeping the system strong: bigger computers, better protection against fraud, and help for customers when something goes wrong. Part of it is meant for a fund to bring more small shops onto UPI.

Not everyone is happy. Some traders' groups have raised concerns, and some have asked to be left out of the rule.

This is not a simple argument. Running UPI costs money, and nobody disagrees with that. The question is who should pay: the shops, the banks, or the government, which in the end means everyone. ₹12.80 on one dinner is small. A few such tables every night, in every restaurant, in every city, is not.

Something to think about

When something is free to use, who do you think is paying for it?

The same restaurant, two bills
Downstairs: idli, ₹50Slice ₹0
Upstairs: dinner for eight, ₹3,200Slice ₹12.80

7What nextPip · The Six

Listen for the Speaker

The speaker on the counter will sound exactly the same on the day the new slice begins. "Received fifty rupees." Nothing about it will tell you that a rule changed that morning.

For six years, from January 2020, shops paid nothing to be paid by UPI. Under the new rule, some of them will pay a little, on their bigger bills. What is still being decided is when.

So the story is not over. Here is what to look out for.

Watch this space
  1. 15 October 2026, or 1 January 2027?NPCI set the first date for the new slice to begin. On 9 October 2026, it was weighing a delay to the second. Watch which one it turns out to be. Then ask a shopkeeper you know whether anything changed for them.
  2. The first days of November 2026.NPCI publishes its numbers for each month soon after the month ends. August 2026 had 24.51 billion payments. September 2026 had 24.07 billion. Will October 2026 be higher or lower?
  3. The first one-billion day.In September 2026, India crossed 800 million UPI payments a day for the first time. One billion in a single day has not happened yet. Watch for it.

Six questions. Five answers. One is still open: who should pay for the two seconds? Nobody has settled it yet. That one is yours to keep asking.
